title: HTTP Requests
body:
Interview prep note. Everything here is framed around one question: **which machine does this happen on?**

## Core Facts to Know

- [[HTTP]] is a request/response protocol.
- HTTP is a [[Stateless Protocol]] — each request is self-contained and unconnected to previous ones.
- The method, [[URL]], headers, and body are all chosen by your machine's [[JavaScript]] before any network activity happens.
- [[DNS]] resolution happens over UDP, not HTTP.
- DNS resolution happens before a single HTTP byte is sent.
- Your machine checks its browser DNS cache first, then the OS DNS cache.
- A recursive DNS resolver is a third-party machine, owned by neither you nor the destination.
- The recursive resolver queries root, then TLD, then authoritative nameservers.
- A resolved [[IP Address]] is cached locally according to the DNS record's TTL.
- The [[TCP Three-Way Handshake]] is SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK.
- The TCP handshake usually terminates at the destination's [[Load Balancer]], not at the final app server.
- The [[TLS Handshake]] happens after the TCP handshake and before any HTTP bytes.
- The response reuses the already-open TCP/TLS connection, so no second handshake is needed.
- **GET** is read-only, safe to cache, and safe to retry.
- **POST** creates something and is not idempotent.
- **PUT** is a full replace and is [[Idempotent]].
- **PATCH** is a partial update and is not guaranteed idempotent.
- **DELETE** removes a resource and is idempotent in intent.
- **HEAD** is a GET that returns headers only, with no body.
- **OPTIONS** is sent automatically by the browser as a [[Preflight Request]], not by your JS code.
- The client chooses the HTTP method; the server must have a registered handler for it or it returns 404/405.
- The URL fragment (`#section`) is stripped by the browser and never reaches the server.
- The query string is sent to the server and shows up in server logs.
- The hostname is re-read by the server as the `Host` header, because one server often answers for many domains.
- **1xx** status codes are informational.
- **2xx** means success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content).
- **3xx** means redirect (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified).
- **4xx** means the client made a mistake (400, 401, 403, 404, 429).
- **5xx** means the server made a mistake (500, 502, 503).
- All status codes are generated on the server, even the 4xx ones that describe your mistake.
- 401 means the server could not verify who you are at all.
- 403 means the server verified who you are, and that identity still isn't allowed.
- 502 Bad Gateway means their load balancer got a bad response from their own app server behind it.
- [[HTTPS]] provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
- The padlock icon only means the connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the domain.
- The padlock says nothing about whether the site itself is trustworthy.
- A [[Certificate Authority]] is a trusted third party that signs the server's certificate.
- IPv4 is 32-bit, has ~4.3 billion addresses, and is already globally exhausted.
- IPv6 is 128-bit and functionally unlimited.
- A private IP like `192.168.x.x` is only meaningful inside your own network.
- [[NAT]] on your router rewrites your private IP to one public IP on the way out.
- [[CORS]] is enforced by your browser, not by the server.

## Core analogy: Sending a letter through a postal system

Running example throughout: you typing this message and hitting Send.

| (Analogy) Postal Step | HTTP/networking term | Where it actually happens |
|---|---|---|
| You write the letter and decide what kind of errand it is (deliver new mail, ask for a copy, etc.) | JS builds the request: method, URL, headers, body via `fetch()`/`XMLHttpRequest` | **Your machine** — the browser's JS engine (e.g. V8), inside that tab's renderer process |
| You hand the sealed letter to the postal service's local counter | `fetch()` hands the request off from JS to the browser's networking layer | **Your machine** — a separate part of the browser (Chrome's network process), not JavaScript itself |
| You check your personal address book for the recipient's street address | DNS cache check | **Your machine** — browser DNS cache, then OS-level DNS cache |
| Your address book doesn't have it, so you call directory assistance | DNS query sent | Travels from your machine, over UDP, to a **recursive DNS resolver** — a third-party machine (your ISP's, or a public one like `8.8.8.8`) not owned by you or the destination |
| Directory assistance calls the city registrar, then the street registrar, to get the final address | Recursive resolver queries root → TLD → authoritative nameservers | **The network in between** — a chain of separate servers, none of which are yours or the destination's |
| You now have the destination's street address | IP address returned and cached | **Your machine** — cached by OS/browser, respecting the DNS record's TTL |
| A courier physically confirms they've reached the right building and opens a channel before handing anything over | TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) | Starts at **your machine's OS network stack**, travels through **your router** (NAT), **your ISP**, and **backbone routers**, ends at the **destination's infrastructure** (often a load balancer, not the final app server) |
| Both sides agree on a secret code so no one along the route can read the letter | TLS handshake (certificate exchange, key negotiation) | Negotiated between **your browser's networking/crypto layer** and the **server's TLS termination point** |
| The actual sealed letter is handed over and carried along the route | HTTP request bytes sent (request line, headers, body) | Travels **your machine → router → ISP → backbone routers → destination's load balancer** |
| The letter arrives at the front desk, which routes it to the right department | Load balancer/reverse proxy routes request to a backend server | **Their machine(s)** — infrastructure the destination company controls |
| The department opens the letter, does the requested work, checks the file room if needed, and writes a reply | Application server parses the request, runs business logic, may query a database, builds a response | **Their machine(s)** — app server, and separately, the database server |
| The reply travels back along the same already-open channel, no new handshake needed | Response sent back over the existing TCP/TLS connection | **Their machine(s) → backbone routers → your ISP → your router → your machine** |
| You open the reply and act on it | Browser resolves the `fetch()` Promise; JS reads the JSON body and updates the page | **Your machine** — back in the JS engine/renderer process, which then updates the [[DOM]] and repaints the screen |

Two things worth stating outright if asked: the method, URL, and body are all decided by **your machine's JavaScript, before any network activity happens** — nothing downstream chooses them. And DNS resolution happens over UDP, a completely separate protocol from HTTP, before a single HTTP byte is sent.

See [[Fetch]] for how the request is actually written in JS, and [[Asynchronous JS]] for why the rest of your code keeps running while it's in flight.

## Methods: who decides, and where

See also [[HTTP Verb]].

| Method | What it means | Where the decision is made |
|---|---|---|
| **GET** | Read-only, no side effects, safe to cache and retry | Decided by the **client-side code** (frontend engineer's `fetch()` call); the **server's router** must have a matching handler or it returns 404/405 |
| **POST** | Creates something; not idempotent | Same split — client chooses it, server must have a registered handler expecting it |
| **PUT** | Full replace; idempotent | Client decides, server must implement replace semantics |
| **PATCH** | Partial update; not guaranteed idempotent | Client decides, server must implement partial-update logic |
| **DELETE** | Remove; idempotent in intent | Client decides, server must implement deletion |
| **HEAD** | Like GET, headers only, no body | Client decides — used to check existence/size cheaply |
| **OPTIONS** | "What are you allowed to send me?" | Sent automatically **by the browser itself**, not by your JS code, as a CORS preflight before certain cross-origin requests (see [[Cookies and Browser Storage]]) |

## URLs, broken into every part, with where each part is read

`https://www.example.com:443/products/search?query=shoes&page=2#reviews`

| Part | Postal equivalent | Where it's read |
|---|---|---|
| `https` | The delivery service used (encrypted vs. not) | **Your machine** — browser decides TLS behavior/default port before any network call |
| `www.example.com` | The building's street address | **The network** — DNS resolvers turn this into an IP; also re-read by the **server** as the `Host` header, since one server often answers for many domains |
| `:443` | The mail slot number | **Your machine's OS TCP stack**, to know which port to open |
| `/products/search` | The department inside the building | **Their machine** — server's router picks a handler based on this |
| `?query=shoes&page=2` | A note clipped to the letter | **Their machine** — sent to and read by the server, also visible in server logs (see [[Query String]]) |
| `#reviews` | A sticky note for you only | **Your machine only** — stripped by the browser before sending; never reaches the server |

## Status codes: who generates them and where

See [[HTTP Status Code]] for the individual codes.

| Code range | Meaning | Where it's generated |
|---|---|---|
| **1xx** | Informational, processing | **Their machine** — rare to encounter directly |
| **2xx** | Success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content) | **Their machine** — set by the application code once it finishes handling the request |
| **3xx** | Redirect (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified) | **Their machine** — server or CDN edge deciding the client should look elsewhere or reuse its cache |
| **4xx** | Client-side mistake (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests) | **Their machine** generates the code, but it's describing a problem with what **your machine** sent |
| **5xx** | Server-side mistake (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable) | **Their machine** — 502 specifically means their load balancer got a bad response from their own app server behind it |

401 vs 403, precisely: 401 means the server couldn't verify who you are at all (missing/invalid credentials). 403 means it verified exactly who you are, and that identity still isn't allowed to do this. See [[Authentication]] vs [[Authorization]].

## HTTPS, mapped

| Guarantee | What it protects against | Where it's enforced |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Anyone on the backbone routers in between reading your message text | Encryption negotiated between **your browser** and the **server's TLS endpoint** during the handshake |
| Integrity | Anyone tampering with the letter in transit undetected | Same handshake — tampering breaks the cryptographic checksum |
| Authentication | An impostor pretending to be the real server | A **[[Certificate Authority]]**, a separate trusted third party, signs the server's certificate; your browser checks that chain of trust |

The padlock icon only confirms the connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the domain — it says nothing about whether the site itself is trustworthy.

## Modern issues, mapped

| Issue | What it is | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| [[CORS]] | Browser blocking JS from reading a cross-origin response | Enforced entirely by **your browser** — the request often still reaches and executes on **their server** |
| HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 | How many requests share a connection, and what transport underlies it | A protocol negotiated between **your browser** and **their server/load balancer** during connection setup |
| Caching headers (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`) | Whether the browser can skip the round trip entirely | Checked by **your machine** before it sends a request; the `ETag` fingerprint is generated by **their server** (see [[HTTP Caching]]) |
| [[CDN]] | A geographically closer copy of static content | A third machine — **neither strictly yours nor the origin server**, run by the CDN provider, often physically near you |

## IP addresses, mapped

| Concept | What it is | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 32-bit address, ~4.3 billion possible, already exhausted globally | Assigned to machines by ISPs/registries across **the network**, not chosen locally |
| IPv6 | 128-bit address, functionally unlimited | Same — assigned across the network, built to solve IPv4 exhaustion |
| Private IP | Address like `192.168.x.x`, meaningful only inside your home network | **Your machine**, assigned by **your router** |
| Public IP | The one address your household presents to the internet | **Your router**, via [[NAT]] — it rewrites your private IP to this on the way out, and keeps a translation table to route replies back to the correct device inside your home |

---
Part of [[Web Interview Prep]].
